svg.aria-label: Diagram: how global and regional network firewall policies differ in scope, with global applying to all regions of a VPC network and regional to one region, and only regional covering RoCE networks; the network firewall policy enforcement order attribute that decides whether these policies are evaluated before or after classic VPC firewall rules, and which steps cannot be moved; how the rule language itself changes inside a policy, with unique priorities, secure tags instead of network tags, service accounts valid as targets but not sources, and Layer 7 inspection unavailable in regional policies; and how quota stops counting rules and starts counting rule attributes, with an FQDN object costing sixty-four
svg.title: Global and regional network firewall policies: two scopes, one switch, and a different rule language
svg.text: These policies live in a project, and one network attribute decides when they are evaluated.
Inside them the rule language is not the VPC firewall rule language, and neither is the quota.
Two policy types, two scopes, both inside one project
GLOBAL: a container resource defined within a project, applying to ALL REGIONS of a network.
Associate it with MANY VPC networks in the same project — but each network gets only ONE.
REGIONAL: per-project, PER-REGION objects, enforced in one region of one or more networks.
Regional is the only one that also covers RoCE networks: VPC_POLICY or RDMA_ROCE_POLICY.
Neither supports target networks. That stays hierarchical-only — #73’s closing finding.
The one step in the evaluation order you are allowed to move
AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL (default): classic VPC firewall rules are evaluated FIRST.
BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL: these policies are evaluated before the VPC firewall rules.
It is an attribute of the NETWORK, not of the policy: networkFirewallPolicyEnforcementOrder.
Hierarchical and regional system policies always run before everything else. Not movable.
Within the policies the order is fixed: global, then regional, then the implied action.
A policy is not a wrapper — the rule language itself changes
PRIORITY must be UNIQUE within a policy. VPC firewall rules allow duplicate priorities.
Tag type is the SECURE TAG, not the network tag. #72’s comparison does not transfer here.
Service accounts work as TARGETS but not as SOURCES. VPC firewall rules allow both.
apply_security_profile_group cannot be used in regional network firewall policies, so
Layer 7 inspection belongs to hierarchical and global policies only.
Priority range is unchanged: an integer from 0 to 2,147,483,547, inclusive.
Quota stops counting rules and starts counting attributes
VPC firewall rules are capped by RULE COUNT. Policies are capped by ATTRIBUTE COUNT.
One IP range, one protocol, one port or port range — one attribute each. An address group
costs the sum of its capacity. An FQDN object costs 64.
Google’s own worked example: 3 + 1 + 64 + 1 + 1 = 70 attributes, for ONE rule.
Target secure tags are not counted at all. The expensive rule is the one with an FQDN.
Regional SYSTEM policies are a fourth kind: Google creates them when a Google service needs
rules in a region, you cannot edit a rule except to toggle logging, more than one can attach
to a region, and you are not charged for evaluating them.
Creating needs Compute Security Admin. ASSOCIATING needs Compute Network Admin — a different
role, so whoever writes the rules is not necessarily whoever can put them into force.
